questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with a severe infection of the face. Which of the following venous structures could allow the infection to spread to the cavernous sinus?

explanation.text: The inferior ophthalmic vein connects the facial veins to the cavernous sinus, making it a route for the spread of infections from the face. Cavernous sinus: It is two large venous spaces situated in the middle cranial fossa, on either side of the body of the sphenoid bone.

Important structures related to Cavernous Sinus: Tributaries or Incoming Channels From the orbit: Superior ophthalmic vein Inferior ophthalmic vein- connects facial vein to cavernous sinus (Option B) Central vein of the retina- drains either into the superior ophthalmic vein or directly into the cavernous sinus.

From the brain: Superficial middle cerebral vein Inferior cerebral veins from the temporal lobe From the meninges Sphenoparietal sinus Frontal trunk of the middle meningeal- drains into the pterygoid plexus or the sphenoparietal or cavernous sinus Draining Channels or Communications Into the transverse sinus through the superior petrosal sinus. (Option A ruled out) Into the internal jugular vein through the inferior petrosal sinus. (Option C ruled out) Into the pterygoid plexus of veins through the emissary veins.

Into the facial vein through the superior ophthalmic vein. The right and left cavernous sinuses communicate with each other through the anterior and posterior intercavernous sinuses and the basilar plexus of veins. (Option D ruled out) Note: All these communications are valveless, and blood flows in both directions. Note: The superior ophthalmic vein has bidirectional flow, whereas the inferior ophthalmic vein has unidirectional blood flow.

Dangerous areas of face: (Upper lip and lower part of the nose) The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus through the pterygoid venous plexus, superior ophthalmic vein, and inferior ophthalmic vein. Infections from the face spread in a retrograde direction and cause thrombosis of the cavernous sinus.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with symptoms of headache and visual disturbances. Imaging studies reveal a large clot in the superior sagittal sinus. Which of the following statements about the superior sagittal sinus is correct?

options.A: It drains directly into the internal jugular vein.
options.B: It runs along the midline, attached to the falx cerebri, and drains into the confluence of sinuses.
options.C: It is located in the falx cerebelli and connects with the occipital sinus.
options.D: It receives blood from the diploic veins within the cranial bones.

explanation.text: The superior sagittal sinus runs along the midline, is attached to the falx cerebri, and typically drains into the confluence of sinuses. Dural Venous Sinuses: Anatomical Features and Location: Network of venous channels: Drain blood from the brain and cranial bones. Location: Between endosteal and meningeal layers of the dura mater. Structure: Lined by endothelium, lacks valves and muscular tissue.
Development: Arise from venous plexuses, often retain plexiform structure.

Sinuses and Connections: Sinus Location Drainage Superior sagittal sinus (Option B) Along midline, attached to falx cerebri (Option C ruled out) Confluence of sinuses, usually right side (Option A ruled out) Inferior sagittal sinus Lower edge of falx cerebri Continues as straight sinus Straight sinus Junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli Drains into left transverse sinus Transverse sinuses Along tentorium cerebelli Continue as sigmoid sinuses Sigmoid sinuses From transverse sinuses Becomes internal jugular vein Occipital sinus In falx cerebelli Drains into confluence of sinuses Cavernous sinuses Plexiform, on either side of sphenoid bone Receives blood from ophthalmic veins, drains via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses Intercavernous sinuses Connects the two cavernous sinuses - Superior petrosal sinuses Drains cavernous sinus into transverse sinus - Inferior petrosal sinuses Drains cavernous sinus into internal jugular vein - Sphenoparietal sinuses Under lesser wings of sphenoid bone Drains into cavernous sinus Basilar sinus and plexus Over clivus, connects cavernous and petrosal sinuses - Marginal sinus Encircles foramen magnum Connects with basilar plexus and occipital sinus Tributaries: Cerebral veins: Drain brain parenchyma.

Diploic veins: Within cranial bones. (Option D ruled out- The superior sagittal sinus does not receive blood from diploic veins; these veins are tributaries to other sinuses. ) Meningeal veins: Drain dura mater. Emissary veins: Connect intracranial and extracranial veins. Clinical Significance: Spread of infection: Emissary veins can facilitate infection spread from extracranial sites to sinuses.

Venous sinus thrombosis: Blood clots can obstruct drainage, leading to complications such as venous infarction and hemorrhage. Surgical considerations: Knowledge of sinus anatomy is crucial for avoiding injury and hemorrhage during neurosurgery. Additional Insights:

Variability: Sinus size and connections can vary, especially in infancy. Imaging techniques: Angiography, MR venography, and CT venography are vital for visualizing sinuses and variations. Innervation: Cranial dura mater is mainly innervated by trigeminal nerve and upper cervical nerves, explaining headache symptoms from dura stimulation.

questions.question: A 56-year-old patient presents with difficulty speaking, swallowing, and hoarseness of voice. On examination, there is noticeable wasting of one side of the tongue and weakness in the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. The patient also exhibits contralateral hemiplegia and contralateral loss of sensation. Which of the following lesions is most likely responsible for these symptoms?

explanation.text: Medullary infarct is the most likely cause as it affects the medulla oblongata, leading to symptoms like bulbar palsy (difficulty speaking and swallowing), tongue wasting, muscle weakness, contralateral hemiplegia, and loss of sensation. These are consistent with the involvement of both ascending and descending tracts through the medulla.

Lower Brainstem Lesions Lower brainstem lesions affect the medulla oblongata and can lead to various neurological symptoms. These are often seen as bulbar palsy. Common Symptoms: Dysarthria: Difficulty speaking due to impaired control of tongue, lips, and vocal cords. Dysphagia (CN IX): Difficulty swallowing caused by weakened throat muscles. Dysphonia: Voice problems, such as hoarseness.

Tongue Wasting (CN XII): Shrinkage and weakness of one side of the tongue, leading to deviation. Muscle Weakness/Wasting: Affects sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles (CN XI), impacting head turning and shoulder elevation. Additional Symptoms: Contralateral Hemiplegia: Paralysis or weakness on the opposite side of the body due to corticospinal tract involvement.

Contralateral Hemianesthesia: Loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body from anterolateral system or dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway involvement. Cerebellar Signs: Coordination and balance difficulties from cerebellar afferent or efferent pathway damage. Nystagmus: Involuntary eye movements indicating vestibular pathway disruptions.

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia: Impaired horizontal eye movements due to medial longitudinal fasciculus lesions. Causes: Space-Occupying Tumours: Examples include meningiomas, vestibular schwannomas, or metastatic carcinomas. Intrinsic Diseases: Gliomas: Tumours from glial cells. Demyelination: Such as in multiple sclerosis. Stroke: Resulting from blood flow interruption.

**Multiple sclerosis (Option A):** primarily causes demyelination and could present with various neurological symptoms but is less likely to produce isolated medullary symptoms with the specific combination of deficits described.
**Meningioma of the cerebellum (Option B):** would more likely cause cerebellar symptoms rather than a specific combination of bulbar palsy and contralateral deficits.
**Vestibular schwannoma (Option D):** typically presents with hearing loss and balance issues rather than the described bulbar symptoms and contralateral deficits.

questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the corticonuclear tract?

options.A: It terminates exclusively in the spinal cord with an ipsilateral projection.
options.B: It descends through the internal capsule and pons, terminating on cranial nerve nuclei with a contralateral projection.
options.C: It controls involuntary movements of the head and neck muscles.
options.D: The term "corticobulbar" is more accurate than "corticonuclear" for describing its function.

explanation.text: The corticonuclear tract fibres descend from the cerebral cortex through the internal capsule and pons. They then terminate on cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem. The fibres exhibit a contralateral projection pattern, meaning they cross the midline of the brainstem to innervate the nuclei on the opposite side of the brainstem.

Corticonuclear Tract: Origin and Pathway: Arises from neurons in the cerebral cortex Descends through: (Option B) Subcortical white matter Genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule Ventral midbrain (crus cerebri) Pons (fragmented into fascicles by pontocerebellar fibers) Termination: (Option A ruled out) Unlike corticospinal fibres, terminates on cranial nerve nuclei and brainstem nuclei: (Option B) Midbrain Pons Medulla oblongata In the medulla, projects to: Nucleus ambiguus Hypoglossal nucleus Exhibits a contralateral projection pattern (crosses midline to opposite brainstem side) Function: Controls voluntary movements (Option C ruled out) of head and neck muscles, including: Facial expression Chewing Swallowing Tongue movement Speech Terminology: (Option D ruled out) "Bulbar" (from "bulb," an outdated term for medulla oblongata) is less accurate than "corticonuclear" "Corticonuclear" is preferred as it covers a broader range of brainstem nuclei beyond the medulla

questions.question: At the level of the facial colliculus, the fibres of which cranial nerves form a loop around the abducens nucleus, creating the colliculus?

explanation.text: The fibres of the facial nerve curve dorsally around the abducens nucleus, forming the facial colliculus. Internal Organization of the Pons Section Dorsal Aspect Ventral Aspect Facial Colliculus Level Medial longitudinal fasciculus: beneath fourth ventricle, lateral to median sulcus Medial lemniscus: ovoid bundle in

ventral pontine tegmentum Abducens nucleus: sends fibres ventro-laterally and caudally Trapezoid body fibers and nuclei cross midline along medial lemniscus Facial nerve nucleus: ventral, lateral, caudal to abducens nucleus Central tegmental tract: longitudinally through mid-pontine tegmentum Facial nerve fibres curve dorsally and laterally over abducens nucleus (facial colliculus) (Option C) Pontine nuclei: transverse pontocerebellar fibres form contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle Inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform and juxtarestiform bodies): superolateral to vestibular nuclei Descending fibres (frontopontine, corticospinal, parieto-temporo-occipito-pontine): longitudinally through basal pons Trigeminal Nerve Nuclei Level Superior cerebellar peduncle: lateral wall of fourth ventricle Medial and lateral lemnisci: convex lemniscal arch, separating tegmentum from basal pons Superior medullary velum: roof of fourth ventricle Trapezoid body fibres and nuclei: curve across midline in ventral tegmentum Superior fovea: lateral margin of fourth ventricle, overlies trigeminal nerve nuclei Mesencephalic tract of trigeminal nerve: dorsolateral tegmentum Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option A): This nerve is not involved at the level of the facial colliculus.
**Trigeminal nerve (Option B):** The trigeminal nerve nuclei are located higher in the mid-pons, not at the level of the facial colliculus.
**Hypoglossal nerve (Option D):** This nerve is located in the medulla, not the pons, and does not contribute to the formation of the facial colliculus.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with lesions at the level marked in the midbrain?

explanation.text: The superior colliculus is marked in the above image and all the given syndromes are associated with lesions at this level. Transverse section at level of the superior colliculus in midbrain Grey Matter Oculomotor nerve nucleus with Edinger Westphal nucleus in the ventromedial part. The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the lateral part. Superior colliculus: Afferents from the retina (visual), and various other centres.

Efferents to the spinal cord (tectospinal tract). Reflex movements of the eyes, and the head and neck in response to visual stimuli. Pretectal nucleus: Location: Deep to the superolateral part of the superior colliculus. Afferents from the lateral roots of the optic tract. Efferents to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei of both sides. Part of the pathway for the light reflex and the consensual reflex.
It causes an Argyll Robertson pupil in which the light reflex is lost but the accommodation reflex remains intact. Red nucleus: Afferents from the superior cerebellar

peduncle, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and cerebral cortex. Efferents to the spinal cord (rubrospinal tract), reticular formation, thalamus, olivary nucleus, subthalamic nucleus. Plays a role in inhibitory influence on muscle tone. Substantia nigra White Matter Crus cerebri Tegmentum Tectum shows the posterior commissure connecting the two superior colliculi.

Syndromes associated with lesions at the level of superior colliculus: Weber’s syndrome: Involves III nerve nucleus and corticospinal fibres. Features: Hemiplegia on the opposite side due to the involvement of corticospinal fibres. Pupil points downwards and laterally due to paralysis of the III nerve. Benedikt’s syndrome: Most of the tegmentum of the midbrain is damaged.

Involves medial lemniscus, red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, and fibres of III nerve. Features: Medial lemniscus- Loss of proprioception. III nerve- Pupil points downwards and laterally. Red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle- Tremors and twitching of the opposite side. Parinaud’s syndrome: Lesion of superior colliculi. Features: Weakness of upward gaze and vertical nystagmus due to damage to the superior colliculus.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding lemniscus?

options.A: It is a collection of axons running in the spinal cord
options.B: The lateral lemniscus is a part of the auditory pathway
options.C: Spinal leminiscus is affected in wallenberg syndrome
options.D: Spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature sensation

explanation.text: Lemniscus is a collection of axons running in the brainstem.

**Lemniscus Collection of axons running in the brainstem (Option A):** Four types (MTSL) Medial lemniscus L ateral lemniscus Trigeminal lemniscus Spinal lemniscus Medial lemniscus Continuation of dorsal column (nucleus gracilis and cuneatus) Sensations it carries are: Pressure Vibration Tactile discrimination Stereognosis Conscious proprioception Lateral lemniscus Formed by fibres arising in nuclei lying in close relation to the trapezoid body (superior olivary nucleus and nucleus of trapezoid body). It carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei. (Option B ruled out) Trigeminal lemniscus Contains fibres arising in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve and traveling to the thalamus. Extends into the midbrain, medulla, and the spinal cord Spinal lemniscus Carries pain and temperature. (Option D ruled out) Lateral medullary ischemia- Wallenberg syndrome (Option C ruled out) Occurs due to blockage of posterior inferior cerebellar artery. It supplies areas behind the inferior olivary nucleus. It involves spinal leminiscus (c/l loss of pain and temp from body) and i/l loss of pain and temp from face (due to involvement of spinal nucleus of V nerve Injury to leminiscus always leads to C/l loss of function

questions.question: A 55-year-old man diagnosed with B12 deficiency presents with difficulty maintaining balance. On examination, he shows a loss of vibration and fine touch sensation in his lower limbs, while pain and temperature sensations are intact. Which of the following pathways is most likely affected in this patient?

explanation.text: Tract of Goll (Gracile fasciculus) is a part of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, responsible for transmitting fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the lower limbs. B12 deficiency can lead to subacute combined degeneration, affecting this pathway and causing the sensory deficits seen in the patient.

Tracts of the spinal cord Column Descending tracts Ascending tracts Anterior white column Anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal, medial reticulospinal Anterior spinothalamic Lateral white column Lateral corticospinal, rubrospinal, lateral reticulospinal, hypothalamospinal Lateral spinothalamic, anterior spinocerebellar, posterior spinocerebellar, spinotectal Posterior white column(Dorsal column) • Fasciculus gracilis (tract of Goll) • Fasciculus cuneatus (tract of Burdach) Dorsal Column (Posterior Column-Medial Lemniscus Pathway): Category Details Components Fasciculus Gracilis: Carries sensory information from the lower limbs (Option C) Fasciculus Cuneatus: Carries sensory information from the upper limbs Sensations Pressure Tactile discrimination Vibration Conscious Proprioception Stereognosis Neuronal Pathway 1st Order Neuron: Located in the dorsal root ganglion 2nd Order Neuron: Located in the medulla oblongata 3rd Order Neuron: Located in the thalamus Spinothalamic Tract (Spinal Lemniscus System): Category Details Types (Options A & B ruled out) Lateral Spinothalamic Tract: Carries pain and temperature sensations Ventral Spinothalamic Tract: Carries crude touch and pressure sensations Pathway 1st Order Neuron: Located in the dorsal root ganglion 2nd Order Neuron: Located in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord 3rd Order Neuron: Located in the thalamus Pyramidal Tract (Corticospinal Tract): Involved in voluntary motor control (Option D ruled out).

Category Details Types Lateral Corticospinal Tract: Contains about 90% of the corticospinal fibers Ventral Corticospinal Tract: Contains the remaining fibers Function Controls fine and skilled voluntary motor activities, such as threading a needle Works in conjunction with the corticobulbar (corticonuclear) tracts Neuronal Pathway Receives axons from the cerebrum (upper motor neuron, UMN type of fibers) Effects of Damage Damage to Pyramidal System: Causes spastic paralysis of skeletal muscles below the level of the lesion Damage to Lower Motor Neurons: Causes flaccid paralysis at the level of the lesion

questions.question: Which of the following arteries is primarily responsible for supplying the sublenticular part of the internal capsule, which carries auditory fibres?

options.A: Recurrent branch of anterior cerebral artery
options.B: Direct branches from the internal carotid

explanation.text: Sublenticular part of the internal capsule is supplied by the branch of anterior choroidal artery and the branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It carries ascending auditory fibres from temporal lobe to thalamus. Vascular supply of internal capsule Sublenticular part of the internal capsule is supplied by the branch of anterior choroidal artery and branch of posterior cerebral artery.
**Recurrent branch of anterior cerebral artery (Option A):** Supplies anterior limb of the internal capsule.
**Direct branches from the internal carotid (Option B):** Supplies genu of the internal capsule.
**Branch of posterior communicating (Option D):** Supplies genu and part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

questions.question: A 62-year-old presents with sudden-onset left-sided weakness, primarily affecting the arm and face. On examination, he has difficulty with speech, displaying both expressive and receptive aphasia. He also shows left-sided facial drooping and an inability to move his left upper limb effectively. Sensation is relatively intact in his lower limb. Which artery is most likely affected?

explanation.text: The MCA supplies the lateral aspects of the cerebral hemispheres, including the motor and sensory cortices controlling the face, upper limb, and speech areas (in the dominant hemisphere). The patient's symptoms of weakness in the face and arm, combined with aphasia, strongly suggest an MCA stroke, as this artery is responsible for these regions.
An ACA stroke typically affects the lower limbs, and a PCA stroke would more likely present with visual field defects or sensory disturbances.

**Artery Affected Areas Involved Clinical Manifestations Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) (Option A):** Medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, corpus callosum Contralateral weakness and sensory loss (lower limb > upper limb) Urinary incontinence, Personality changes (frontal lobe involvement), Transcortical motor aphasia (dominant hemisphere) Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) (Option C) Lateral surface of the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, basal ganglia, internal capsule Contralateral weakness and sensory loss (face and upper limb > lower limb) Aphasia (dominant hemisphere), Hemineglect (non-dominant hemisphere), Homonymous hemianopia Gaze preference towards the side of the lesion Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) (Option B) Occipital lobe, inferior part of temporal lobe, thalamus Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, Visual agnosia, Thalamic pain syndrome, Cortical blindness (if bilateral), Memory deficits (if temporal lobe is involved)

questions.question: Identify the artery highlighted in blue in the following image.

explanation.text: The anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries and forms part of the Circle of Willis. This artery plays a critical role in allowing collateral blood flow between the left and right sides of the cerebral circulation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with Horner’s syndrome, but notably, the patient does not exhibit anhidrosis. Based on the absence of anhidrosis, which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?

explanation.text: The absence of anhidrosis in Horner's syndrome suggests that the lesion is likely located in the postganglionic (third-order neuron) segment of the oculosympathetic pathway. The sweat glands are primarily innervated by sympathetic fibers that branch off earlier. Hence, in third-order Horner's syndrome, if the disruption occurs after these fibers have already branched off, sweating pathways are unaffected, and anhidrosis does not occur.
In contrast, anhidrosis is always present in first-order or second-order Horner's syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about prevertebral/paravertebral ganglia is/are true? Prevertebral ganglia are also known as collateral ganglia. Prevertebral ganglia are a part of the parasympathetic nervous system. Paravertebral ganglia supply the abdominal viscera. The celiac ganglion is a paravertebral ganglion.

explanation.text: Prevertebral ganglia are also known as collateral ganglia. Prevertebral ganglia and paravertebral ganglia both are part of the sympathetic nervous system, not the parasympathetic nervous system. Paravertebral ganglia (sympathetic trunk ganglia) primarily supply the body wall and limbs, while prevertebral ganglia (e.g., celiac ganglion) supply the abdominal viscera.

The celiac ganglion is a prevertebral (collateral) ganglion, not a paravertebral ganglion. Characteristic Prevertebral Ganglia Paravertebral Ganglia Alternate Names Also known as collateral ganglia or preaortic ganglia. (Statement I) Also known as sympathetic chain ganglia.

Sympathetic Pathway Both are part of the sympathetic nervous system. (Statement II ruled out) Location Anterior to the aorta, close to major arteries like the celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries. Adjacent to the vertebral column, forming sympathetic chains on either side of the spine. Structure Associated with the abdominal aorta and related to major arteries.

Forms a chain along the spine, with ganglia in the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions. Function Supplies abdominal and pelvic organs, controls visceral functions like peristalsis and secretion. (Statement III ruled out) Supplies the thoracic viscera, blood vessels, skin, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles.

Preganglionic Fibers Receive preganglionic fibers from the splanchnic nerves (e.g., greater, lesser, least splanchnic). Receive preganglionic fibers from the spinal cord segments (T1-L2) via white rami communicantes. Postganglionic Fibers Postganglionic fibers form plexuses like the celiac and hypogastric plexus, supplying abdominal and pelvic organs.

Postganglionic fibers distributed via grey rami communicantes to spinal nerves and target skin, blood vessels, and thoracic viscera. Notable Ganglia Includes the celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, and aorticorenal ganglia. (Statement IV ruled out) Includes cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral ganglia, and ganglion impar.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: Preganglionic fibers in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are myelinated.
options.B: Postganglionic fibers in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are unmyelinated
options.C: Most sweat glands are sympathetic and adrenergic.
options.D: Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter found in sympathetic ganglia.

explanation.text: Most sweat glands (eccrine) are sympathetic and cholinergic, not adrenergic. Only a few sweat glands (apocrine) are sympathetic and adrenergic.

ANS - Effectors: General Visceral Efferent (GVE) Smooth muscles Cardiac muscles Glands Neurotransmitters and Efferent Innervation: Autonomic Efferent Innervation - GVE Neuron Bodies: Lateral horn cells of the spinal cord Can be sympathetic or parasympathetic neurons Predominantly sympathetic neurons Sacral spinal cord: Parasympathetic neurons are also present Preganglionic Fibers: Myelinated (both in sympathetic and parasympathetic systems) (Option A ruled out) White in color Postganglionic Fibers: Unmyelinated (both in sympathetic and parasympathetic systems) (Option B ruled out) Grey in color Neurotransmitters: Acetylcholine: Found in parasympathetic and sympathetic ganglia (Option D ruled out) Effector Organ Responses: Parasympathetic: Cholinergic (acetylcholine) Sympathetic: Adrenergic (epinephrine and norepinephrine) (rare) Sweat Glands: Most sweat glands (eccrine) are sympathetic and cholinergic Few sweat glands (apocrine) are sympathetic and adrenergic

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness in her left leg. On examination, you observe that her left leg has decreased muscle tone, and shows significant muscle atrophy. Given these findings, which of the following additional signs is likely to be present?

explanation.text: The patient’s findings of decreased muscle tone, muscle atrophy, and flaccid paralysis are indicative of Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) involvement. In LMN lesions, you typically see muscle atrophy and decreased muscle tone along with absent deep tendon reflexes. Fasciculations, which are involuntary muscle twitches, are a common additional sign in LMN lesions due to denervation of the muscle fibers.

Feature LMN Paralysis UMN Paralysis Muscle Tone Decreased Increased Type of Paralysis Flaccid Spastic (Option C ruled out) Muscle Atrophy Occurs later No atrophy Reaction of Degeneration Seen Not seen Tendon Reflexes Absent Exaggerated (Option A ruled out) Side of Affected Body Ipsilateral Contralateral Babinski Sign Negative Positive (Option B ruled out) Fasciculation Present Absent

questions.question: A 35-year-old patient presents following a fall from a ladder. The patient exhibits specific neurological symptoms: loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg, difficulty identifying the position of the right leg with eyes closed, and complete loss of sensation at the T12 level of the trunk on the right. Which of the following statements is false for this condition?

options.A: Loss of proprioception in the right leg occurs due right dorsal column.
options.B: Loss of pain in the left leg occurs due to the left spinothalamic tract.
options.C: Damage to the ventral nerve roots at the T12 level results in loss of sensation.
options.D: Spastic paralysis of the right leg

explanation.text: The patient's presentation is consistent with Brown-Séquard Syndrome, resulting from a hemisection of the spinal cord. In Brown-Séquard syndrome, pain, and temperature sensations are lost on the opposite side of the body from the lesion due to the crossing of the spinothalamic tract fibers. Therefore, loss of pain in the left leg would be due to damage to the right spinothalamic tract, not the left.

Brown-Sequard syndrome Below the Level of Lesion: Ipsilateral Upper Motor Neuron Paralysis: Due to damage to the pyramidal tract (corticospinal tract) (Option D ruled out). Ipsilateral Loss of Conscious Proprioceptive Sensations: Caused by damage to the posterior white column (Option A ruled out). Contralateral Loss of Pain and Temperature Sensations: Due to damage to the lateral spinothalamic tract and anterior spinothalamic tract.

At the Level of Lesion: (Option C ruled out) Ipsilateral Lower Motor Neuron Paralysis: Resulting from damage to the ventral nerve roots. Ipsilateral Anesthesia Over the Skin of the Segment: Due to injury to the ventral nerve roots. Above the Level of Lesion: Ipsilateral Hyperesthesia: Resulting from irritation of the dorsal nerve roots.

questions.question: A patient presented with vision loss. On radiological investigation, an aneurysm causing damage to the optic chiasma was noted. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the artery that is causing the damage?

explanation.text: Answer A - Anterior communicating artery The optic chiasma is located just above the anterior communicating artery (AComA) in the suprasellar cistern. Aneurysms of the AComA are the most common intracranial aneurysms and can compress the optic chiasma, leading to bitemporal hemianopia (loss of peripheral vision in both eyes). These aneurysms often present with vision loss, headaches, and possibly subarachnoid hemorrhage if they rupture.

Anterior choroidal artery (option B): This artery arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies parts of the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, and posterior limb of the internal capsule. Aneurysms here are rare and typically cause contralateral motor deficits rather than optic chiasma compression. Middle cerebral artery (option C): The MCA does not course near the optic chiasma.

MCA aneurysms more commonly affect the lateral convexity of the brain, leading to contralateral hemiparesis, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), or neglect (non-dominant hemisphere). Anterior cerebral artery (option D): The ACA courses superior to the optic chiasma, but aneurysms at this location usually do not cause direct compression. ACA infarcts more commonly lead to leg weakness (contralateral) due to involvement of the paracentral lobule.

questions.question: Which of the following options are included in the limbic system? 1. Amygdala 2. Hippocampus 3. Thalamus

explanation.text: The limbic system is a collection of brain structures involved in emotion, memory, and motivation. The key components of the limbic system include: Amygdala → Plays a crucial role in emotion processing, particularly fear and aggression. Hippocampus → Essential for learning and memory, particularly long-term memory formation. Other Major Components of the Limbic System: Hypothalamus → Regulates autonomic functions and emotional responses.

Cingulate gyrus → Involved in emotion formation and processing. Mammillary bodies → Associated with memory processing. Thalamus: While the thalamus is important for sensory relay, it is not strictly part of the limbic system. However, some parts of the thalamus (e.g., anterior nucleus and dorsomedial nucleus) are functionally linked to the limbic system.

questions.question: Identify the cranial nerve that arises from the marked part.

explanation.text: The abducens nerve (CN VI) arises from the pontomedullary junction, specifically from the ventral surface of the brainstem, near the midline. It travels forward to innervate the lateral rectus muscle, which controls abduction of the eye (lateral movement).

Attachment of the nerves to the brain: 1, 2 - Forebrain 3- Arises from ventral midbrain 4- Dorsal midbrain (cannot see its origin in the Anterior view of the brainstem) 5- Lateral pons 6, 7, 8- Ponto medullary junction (from medial to lateral respectively) 9, 10, 11- Lateral to olives (from superior to inferior respectively) 12- Between pyramid and olives Oculomotor nerve (option A): The oculomotor nerve (CN III) arises from the midbrain (interpeduncular fossa), not the pontomedullary junction.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (option B): The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) emerges from the medulla, specifically the postolivary sulcus, above the vagus nerve, not from the pontomedullary junction. Facial nerve (option D): The facial nerve (CN VII) also arises from the pontomedullary junction, but it is located laterally, near the cerebellopontine angle. The abducens nerve is more medial, while the facial nerve is lateral to it.

questions.question: Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway of the basal ganglia:- 1. Striatum 2. Globus pallidus 3. Substantia nigra 4. Thalamus 5. Cortex

explanation.text: Cortex (5) → Initiates movement and sends excitatory signals to the striatum. Striatum (1) (Caudate + Putamen) → Receives input from the cortex and modulates basal ganglia output. Globus pallidus (2) (Internal and External segments) → Affects the output to the thalamus. Substantia nigra (3) (Pars compacta and Pars reticulata) → Modulates the activity of the striatum and globus pallidus.

Thalamus (4) → Relays processed signals back to the cortex for movement execution. Direct Pathway: Promotes movement by reducing inhibitory output from the GPi to the thalamus. Mechanism: The striatum inhibits the GPi, leading to less inhibition of the thalamus and increased motor activity. Indirect Pathway: Inhibits movement by increasing inhibitory output from the GPe to the thalamus.

Mechanism: The striatum inhibits the GPe, resulting in less inhibition of the STN, which then excites the GPi. This increased activity of the GPi leads to more inhibition of the thalamus and decreased motor activity.
